Question 1
?

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2−2dydx−8y=6e4x.

a
y=Ae−2x+Be4x−2xe4x
b
y=Ae−2x+Be4x−2e4x
c
y=Ae−x+Be2x+e4x
d
y=Ae−2x+Be4x+xe4x
e
y=Ae−x+Be2x+2e4x
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation r^2-2r-8=(r+2)(r-4)=0 gives y_h=Ae^{-2x}+Be^{4x}. Because e^{4x} is a homogeneous solution, try y_p=Cxe^{4x}. Substitution gives y_p''-2y_p'-8y_p=6Ce^{4x}, so C=1. Thus option d is the general solution.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8y=6{e}^{4x}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =4$,  hence the complementary function ${y}_{c}$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{4x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $4$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (8+16x){e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (8+16x){e}^{4x}-2(\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x})-8\alpha x{e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ (8+16x-2-8x-8x)\alpha {e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 6\alpha {e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 6\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{4x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}+x{e}^{4x}.
$$

Find the general solution to the equation d2ydx2−2dydx−8y=6e4x.

a
y=Ae−2x+Be4x−2xe4x

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the complementary function yc(x), which is the solution to the homogeneous equation d2ydx2−2dydx−8y=0.

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives: λ2−2λ−8=0(λ+2)(λ−4)=0

So λ=−2 or λ=4, hence the complementary function yc is yc=Ae−2x+Be4x.

We now need to find the particular integral yp(x).

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is 6e4x. In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is 4, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form yp=αxe4x, where α is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of yp gives dypdx=α(1+4x)e4x,d2ypdx2=α(8+16x)e4x.

We substitute yp, yp′, and yp″ into the ODE and solve for α: α(8+16x)e4x−2(α(1+4x)e4x)−8αxe4x=6e4x(8+16x−2−8x−8x)αe4x=6e4x6αe4x=6e4x6α=6α=1

Therefore, yp(x)=xe4x.

The general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), and therefore, the general solution in our case is y=Ae−2x+Be4x+xe4x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Linearly Dependent
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8y=6{e}^{4x}.
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =4$,  hence the complementary function ${y}_{c}$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{4x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $4$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (8+16x){e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (8+16x){e}^{4x}-2(\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x})-8\alpha x{e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ (8+16x-2-8x-8x)\alpha {e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 6\alpha {e}^{4x} & =6{e}^{4x} \\ 6\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{4x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{4x}+x{e}^{4x}.
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation r^2+7r+12=(r+3)(r+4)=0 gives the complementary solution Ae^{-3x}+Be^{-4x}. For a particular solution Ce^{3x}, substitution gives (9+21+12)Ce^{3x}=21e^{3x}, so C=1/2. Therefore option b is the general solution.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=21{e}^{3x}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+7\lambda +12 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-4$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $21{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=3\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=9\alpha {e}^{3x}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p}$, ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{3x}+7(3\alpha {e}^{3x})+12(\alpha {e}^{3x}) & =21{e}^{3x} \\ (9+21+12)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =21{e}^{3x} \\ 42\alpha  & =21 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=21{e}^{3x}.
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+7\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+7\lambda +12 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-4$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $21{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=3\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=9\alpha {e}^{3x}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p}$, ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\alpha {e}^{3x}+7(3\alpha {e}^{3x})+12(\alpha {e}^{3x}) & =21{e}^{3x} \\ (9+21+12)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =21{e}^{3x} \\ 42\alpha  & =21 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

Question 3

Solve the initial value problem y″−4y′+8y=20e2x,y(0)=1,  y′(0)=2.

a
y=e2x(cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x)+5e2x
b
y=−4e2xcos⁡2x+5e2x
c
y=e2x(−2cos⁡2x+4sin⁡2x)−e2x
d
y=3e2xsin⁡x+e2x
e
y=e2x(3cos⁡x+2sin⁡x)+5e2x
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic roots are 2±2i, so y=e^{2x}(A cos(2x)+B sin(2x))+5e^{2x}. The particular term follows from (4-8+8)·5=20. Then y(0)=A+5=1 gives A=-4, and y'(0)=2(A+5)+2B=2 gives B=0. Thus option b satisfies the equation and both initial conditions.

after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8=0\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2,$ which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-4(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =20{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha (4-8+8){e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =5\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+5{e}^{2x}.
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+10{e}^{2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2P+2Q+10 & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-4$ and $Q=0.$

We substitute this into the general particular integral and find that the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+0)+5{e}^{2x} \\  & =-4{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+5{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore,  the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2,$ which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-4(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =20{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha (4-8+8){e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =5\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{e}^{2x}.
$$

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives:

$$

$$

$$

after.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=10{e}^{x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x},$ we have that $\lambda =1$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $1$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ({x}^{2}+2x){e}^{x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha ({x}^{2}+4x+2){e}^{x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha ({x}^{2}+4x+2){e}^{x}-2(\alpha ({x}^{2}+2x){e}^{x})+(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{x}) & =10{e}^{x} \\ ({x}^{2}+4x+2-2{x}^{2}-4x+{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{x} & =10{e}^{x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{x} & =10{e}^{x} \\ 2\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{x}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$

after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4{e}^{2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{2x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
after.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+B{e}^{2x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =1$ and $\lambda =2.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{2x}.
$$

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+2x){e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (4x+4){e}^{2x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (4x+4){e}^{2x}-3(\alpha (1+2x){e}^{2x})+2(\alpha x{e}^{2x}) & =4{e}^{2x} \\ (4x+4-3-6x+2x)\alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha {e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4x{e}^{2x}.
$$
